items.title: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin
items.summary:
The role AI played in job losses at Australia’s NAB, Qantas, Canva and Atlassian is far from clear – but it may prove to have more impact on the stock market than the jobs market

  • Get our breaking news email, free app or daily news podcast

In 1987, the Nobel prize winning economist Robert Solow remarked: “You can see the computer age everywhere but in the productivity statistics.” At the time, computers had been around for 40 years. Real productivity gains did emerge in the 1990s after the arrival of the internet, but they were short-lived.

Four years after the launch of ChatGPT, the pattern seems to be much the same: lots of hype and excitement but with very little productivity growth. The main economic impacts, as in the 1990s dotcom era, have been a stock market boom and huge investment in infrastructure (fibre optics then, datacentres today), betting on future demand that has yet to emerge.

items.t: Is the AI job apocalypse finally here? The evidence suggests otherwise | John Quiggin

items.title: Skims’ $148 advent calendar flop wasn’t a stunt, marketers say—but store credit may not win back Kim Kardashian’s angry customers
items.summary:
“We might be on track for the worst advent calendar I’ve ever opened,” content creator Kayla Ryan said in a TikTok video this week, referring to the $148 Skims 12-day advent calendar that customers have been ripping apart for the past several days. 

“I could get these at Dollar Tree ,” she continued, pulling three unpacked hair ties from the day three slot on the advent calendar. The $148 box held keychains, bobby pins, scrunchies, and hair ties—but none of the bodysuits or loungewear that made Kim Kardashian’s company so popular.

Countless videos like Ryan’s have flooded social media for the past several days, prompting Skims to scramble to contain the fallout. In response to the online outrage, the company “personally contacted every customer who purchased the calendar and offered them a choice of a full refund or a SKIMS credit to put towards other products,” a spokesperson told other outlets. 

Skims did not respond to multiple requests for comment from Fortune .

The catch, according to the email buyers received, is that a cash refund means sending the calendar back, while shoppers who opt for store credit keep it. That detail led to some theories that Skims had purposefully rage-baited customers.

“Skims knew what they were doing with that advent calendar. I’d bet money it was intentional,” Jessica Tillery, a senior vice president of brand communications for Allison Worldwide, wrote in a LinkedIn post this week.

“Every dollar spent over that $148 credit is new revenue for them,” Tillery wrote. “Every person who comes back to shop with that credit is a repeat…
items.t: Skims’ $148 advent calendar flop wasn’t a stunt, marketers say—but store credit may not win back Kim Kardashian’s angry customers

items.title: Bodyguards aren’t enough: After Jensen Huang’s exit, CEOs need counterintelligence training
items.summary:
This month, Jensen Huang resigned as CEO of Nvidia after acknowledging an affair with a woman U.S. intelligence officials suspect is a Chinese intelligence asset. Nvidia’s board said it had “no reason to believe that either national security or NVIDIA secrets were compromised,” and China has denied the allegations.

A month earlier, OpenAI’s countermeasures team found a listening device in a San Francisco conference room where executives often held sensitive discussions. The FBI later arrested an OpenAI employee accused of planting it .

To most people, espionage belongs in spy thrillers. For C-suite executives, corporate espionage and executive targeting are a growing threat. Companies once seen as untouchable now face foreign espionage and physical targeting.

The problem isn’t awareness or money. Today’s executives have to change how they live, travel, and interact with the people around them to prepare for adversaries.

Big tech companies already spend millions on executive security. Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, spent nearly $4 million protecting Huang in fiscal 2026, according to Fortune ‘s analysis of company filings , up from $3.5 million in 2024 .

The December 2024 killing of UnitedHealthcare CEO Brian Thompson on a Manhattan sidewalk reminded S&P 500 companies that security reaches well beyond cybersecurity. Since then, spending has climbed. About 38% of S&P 500 companies provided security perks to at least some executives in 2025, up from 28% in 2023, according to an early look at proxy filings by executive data firm Equilar .

AI companies are a…
items.t: Bodyguards aren’t enough: After Jensen Huang’s exit, CEOs need counterintelligence training

items.title: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it
items.summary:
“Raise your hand if your executive team has mandated the use of AI.”

I was standing on stage at the annual Great Places to Work convention in Las Vegas, and every one of the 500 CHROs I was in front of put their hands up. These were all HR leaders in mid-market and enterprise companies.

“Now, keep your hands up if every single person on your executive team is using AI to make themselves more valuable.”

Almost every hand went down.

I ask this question at every speaking engagement, and I’ve seen a pattern–and a problem. Company leaders are mandating the use of AI. With that mandate, they’re expecting increases in the productivity of their workforce. But they’re not holding themselves to the same standard.

Executives often think that “leading AI” in their organizations means delegating the adoption and strategy of it to IT, a Chief AI Officer, or an outside consultant. That’s not delegation–that’s abdication.

CEOs and executive teams need to learn to use AI, and become AI-driven leaders, before they can build AI-driven organizations.

I say this as I’m starting to see companies increasingly tying AI goals and skills directly to employee raises and promotions. Should compensation be tied to AI skill? It depends on the company. If you’re an organization that typically ties performance to specific skills that will grow in value, it makes sense. If you don’t, it’s a break from precedent–but it doesn’t mean it’s the wrong move.

What does concern me is when a CEO who doesn’t use AI is the one making the call. And by “use AI,” I don’t mean to help them write better emails–I…
items.t: I helped grow a steel company from $750 million to $12 billion. CEOs should use AI before they grade employees on it

items.title: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads
items.summary:
Public universities helped make American higher education a draw for students and researchers worldwide. Now lawmakers and governing boards from Kansas to Utah want proof that the professors who teach there work hard enough.

Faculty say the premise is backward. Professors who spoke with Fortune describe 55-hour weeks, departments that have shrunk by as much as half, and raises that haven’t kept pace with inflation.

“We are losing ground,” said Renita Coleman , a journalism professor at the University of Texas at Austin.

As scrutiny of higher education grows , state legislators, governing boards, and administrators have started questioning how professors spend their time and whether they deliver enough for their salaries and job protections. Some have pushed to limit tenure . Others are demanding a detailed accounting of faculty responsibilities.

Critics see tenure as a shield for underperformers. Faculty say that misreads the job 

Public confidence in American higher education has fallen sharply over the past decade. According to Gallup , 38% of Americans expressed a great deal or quite a lot of confidence in higher education in 2026, down from 57% in 2015. The share expressing very little or no confidence rose from 10% to 25%.

The weakening trust comes amid a convergence of concerns, from rising college costs and questions about the value of degrees to political battles on campuses . Those frustrations have fueled skepticism of tenure, which grants professors permanent faculty status after they meet a university’s standards for teaching, research, and service.…
items.t: ‘We are losing ground’: Professors log 55-hour weeks as pay stagnates and states question their workloads

items.title: Pete Hegseth’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request is DOA after Democrats swept midterms, but global defense spending could still hit $8 trillion
items.summary:
A wave of Democratic midterm victories may have put the kibosh on the Trump administration’s plans to boost the Pentagon’s budget, but global defense spending is expected to top $8 trillion anyway.

Rep. Adam Smith, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, argued in a letter to colleagues that the Defense Department’s proposed $1.5 trillion budget for 2027, a more than 40% increase, was too high and would come at the expense of services to the American people. 

He called for a smaller military budget as well as a probe into the Pentagon’s dealings with defense contractors. 

“We must thoroughly review our national defense strategy and develop a more realistic and sustainable approach that does not require a defense budget in excess of $1 trillion or paid for through draconian cuts to critical domestic programs,” Smith wrote. 

Economists and public policy experts say a growing interest in cybersecurity and rearmament amid ongoing geopolitical conflicts has accelerated a cycle of defense spending that slowed after the Cold War and ramped up again after 9/11. 

According to asset management firm Carlyle , defense spending has increased to 2.0% of the GDP across the G7 countries of Canada, France, Germany, Italy, Japan, the UK, and U.S. That’s the highest share in more than three decades. At the current rate of spending, it could reach 3.8%, or roughly $8 trillion in defense commitments.

The U.S. accounts for about one-third of the world’s defense spending , surging past the $1 trillion mark in fiscal 2026. While it’s by far the biggest spender—providing aid…
items.t: Pete Hegseth’s $1.5 trillion Pentagon budget request is DOA after Democrats swept midterms, but global defense spending could still hit $8 trillion

items.title: From the Lost Generation to Gen Beta: How every generation got its name
items.summary:
Generation Beta had a name before its first members were born. The label for babies born from 2025 through 2039 was already in headlines in late 2024, courtesy of the Australian demographer who also named the generation before it, Gen Alpha .

That is a long way from how this used to work. The Lost Generation got its name secondhand, from a French garage owner, via Gertrude Stein and Ernest Hemingway. A network news anchor named the Greatest Generation more than half a century after it went to war.

There’s no official process for naming a generation; it’s more like a cultural quorum is reached, and a name takes hold, even though it’s never technically fixed. The moniker for tens of millions of people born within a couple of decades of one another can come from a magazine essay, a novel, or a research firm. The only real key to a name sticking is that lots of people start using it.

The labels carry real money. McCrindle, the research firm behind Gen Alpha, projects that cohort will command $5.46 trillion in spending power by 2029 . They also shape how managers size up young workers, a habit one Fortune commentary argued hurts Gen Z at work .

Even the people who measure generations are cautious about the boxes. In 2023, Pew Research Center said it would apply generational labels more selectively , warning that the standard definitions “may be too broad and arbitrary to capture differences that exist among narrower cohorts.”

From a French garage to a news anchor’s bestseller 

The first widely recognized named generation in Western culture was the Lost Generation,…
items.t: From the Lost Generation to Gen Beta: How every generation got its name

items.title: America’s debt problem: why wealthy families should be looking beyond the midterms
items.summary:
America’s issues with its public finances will outlast the political theatre of any midterm election. The midterms will change the balance of power in Washington, but they will not remove the fiscal pressures facing the country.

For wealthy families, the underlying issue is straightforward, namely that a government carrying historic levels of debt, with rising costs of servicing it , will eventually have to confront the question of how to raise more revenue.

Any administration operating with limited room for additional borrowing and spending will have to consider its options, and private wealth, or taxing the income or private wealth of the rich as it will likely be put, will inevitably be part of that conversation.

Taxation is the obvious starting point. Federal decisions on income, capital gains, estate and gift taxes have a direct bearing on how wealth is held, invested and transferred between generations. The current federal estate and gift tax exemptions of $15m per individual, or $30m for married couples, provide considerable scope for planning. But assuming those thresholds, or the wider tax framework, will remain unchanged indefinitely would be a mistake.

For high-net-worth families, the real vulnerability is not simply whether a tax rate increases but whether the structures they have spent years putting in place will continue to work if the rules change. The time to examine those arrangements is before a legislative change makes the decision urgent.

Nor does diversifying wealth necessarily provide protection against these pressures. Many families spread…
items.t: America’s debt problem: why wealthy families should be looking beyond the midterms

items.title: Meet the short seller that flagged Nvidia’s ‘significant China problem’ six months ago—including ‘uncomfortably close’ ties with Alice Huang
items.summary:
Six months ago, Nvidia stock peaked at $235.74 a share. But while others were focused on the AI boom and Nvidia’s growing market cap, one research firm saw a China-sized crack in the foundation.

Now, Nvidia is down 27.9% since then, and Jensen Huang has been ousted as CEO following his romantic affair with a suspected Chinese spy. 

In a report in May, short seller Culper Research raised concerns about Nvidia’s exposure to China—including Huang’s relationship with the suspected spy, Alice Huang.

“This is not a bet against AI. We are short Nvidia for one reason: the Company has a significant China problem,” the report read. 

Culper Research did not immediately respond to a request for comment from Fortune regarding the return on its short bet. 

The China problem 

The central allegation in Culper’s report was that more than 20% of Nvidia’s fiscal 2026 compute revenue was driven by Chinese demand, despite assertions from the company that its China business had fallen to zero following U.S. export restrictions in April 2025.

Culper alleged the revenue came through the smuggling of restricted GPUs to Chinese customers and via Southeast Asian intermediaries that purchased Nvidia hardware and provided computing capacity to Chinese companies.

The research’s allegations focused on Singapore-based Megaspeed International, which it says was secretly financed by China’s Alibaba through a network of shell companies—potentially allowing Chinese companies to access Nvidia’s advanced AI chips.

The problem in relying on this undisclosed China-based revenue was that Beijing has…

items.title: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he’d lost coverage
items.summary:
Eli McCreary of Omaha, Nebraska, said he had recently been diagnosed with kidney cancer when he got a call from a local hospital run by CHI Health. He said he was informed that he wasn’t insured anymore under Medicaid — and that the hospital would cancel his appointments unless he paid out-of-pocket.

McCreary, who was 64 at the time, said he phoned a call center for help. He said he was told his benefits under Medicaid, the government health program for people with low incomes or disabilities, now required that he have a job.

“You’re required to do work to stay on,” McCreary said a representative told him. “And you haven’t fulfilled your work requirement.”

For decades, McCreary said, he has battled drug addiction. A substance use treatment program discharged him in March, and in June he was diagnosed with cancer in his right kidney, according to documents reviewed by KFF Health News . He also has diabetes and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.

“I don’t understand what job I can get,” McCreary said. “I can’t walk. I can hardly breathe. I can’t move around. What job am I going to get?”

McCreary said he canceled a CT scan and other tests at the hospital, which is part of CommonSpirit Health, the nation’s largest Catholic health system. He also delayed a cancer-related appointment with a physician who travels back and forth to Omaha. “I missed my window of opportunity with him for another month,” he said.

Taylor Miller, a spokesperson for CHI Health, declined to answer questions about McCreary’s experience. In an emailed statement she said that “CHI Health is…
items.t: Nebraska rushed Medicaid work rules. Then a cancer patient was told he’d lost coverage

items.title: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI
items.summary:
The latest instalment of the epic crime saga is finally here. We visit Rockstar Games for a hands-on encounter with the cultural event of the decade – and can confirm it more than lives up to the hype

It still comes as a surprise for many to learn that Grand Theft Auto, the brazenly American crime series that has been one of the world’s most popular and most controversial video games for the past 20 years, is mainly made in Scotland. But if you grow up in Edinburgh, developer Rockstar North is part of the background mythology of the place. Plenty of people passed through this studio at some point or another in the 2000s, as game testers or employees. As a student in Edinburgh at that time, I would hear rumours of wild parties at the executives’ houses, as decadent as those in the game. At a bar or a birthday or a housewarming, you might meet a guy who claimed to have come up with one of the puerile puns that grace the in-game businesses (eg Nutsaki, a Japanese restaurant, or the fried-chicken chain Cluckin’ Bell). Grand Theft Auto is now made by a huge team of nearly 5,000 people around the world but its central nervous system is still in Holyrood, in the shadow of Arthur’s Seat.

The setting of the latest Grand Theft Auto game really could not be further from the Scottish capital. Grand Theft Auto VI takes us to Vice City in the state of Leonida, a parody of Miami, Florida. It is a neon-soaked metropolis of sleaze and struggle, hard-partying excess juxtaposed with a barely concealed criminal underworld and unpredictable Florida madness.
items.t: Ten years, thousands of staff and a billion dollars: the exclusive inside story of Grand Theft Auto VI

items.title: $970 million Pacsun CEO says Gen Alpha and Gen Z are ‘greatly misunderstood’—so she made a board of 13- to 22-year-olds to give her advice
items.summary:
Bosses and senior staffers often moan about how young professionals are disengaged and lack initiative . But Brieane Olson, the CEO of Pacsun, warns against overlooking Gen Z and Gen Alpha—and she’s even ensuring they get a seat at the table of the fashion giant that hit $970 million in sales last year. 

“I definitely felt, having spent so much time on the front-line with young consumers, that Gen Z and Gen Alpha were greatly misunderstood,” Olson tells Fortune. “And so, what could we do as a brand that caters to young people to really give them a seat at the table and to build something meaningful and really put community first?”

Once every year, Pacsun’s Youth Advisory Council gathers with company executives to discuss big business concerns. 

The mini board of directors—comprised of 15 Gen Alpha and Gen Zers aged 13 to 22 who are rotated in each year—weigh in on pressing industry needs, what Pacsun should do differently, and the best paths moving forward. 

The country’s youngest minds bring critical feedback directly to Olson and other company executives, touching upon everything from the customer experience to the way stores operate. 

“I think one of the things that has taught me personally about working with this council over the last two years, is really that working with these younger generations requires sometimes giving additional context. And so it’s really important to bring them along for the journey and to answer the whys before they become a why,” the CEO says. “The most important thing is to truly listen—allow to have a dialogue, be a part of the…

items.title: AFC Wimbledon, a failed £87m investment bid and the challenge for fan ownership

When you walk up from Haydons Road train station to Plough Lane there is a blue AFC Wimbledon billboard that reads “Fan owned football”, directly opposite the site of the old Plough Lane stadium where there are now blocks of flats. There is a memorial to the old Wimbledon FC – a reminder that supporters can often have little say in the running of their club – on the same corner, just up the road from the new Cherry Red Records Stadium.

AFC Wimbledon are one of only two majority fan-owned clubs in the EFL – along with Exeter City – but that makes running a loss-making operation, as 94% of teams in England’s top five tiers are doing according to the State of the Game report, even more challenging. “In other clubs, the owner just puts their hand in their pocket, produces cash,” said Hannah Kitcher, who has been a member of the Dons Trust Board (DTB), which runs AFC Wimbledon, for seven years. “It’s harder when the owners are fans – you can only go to them so many times.”

‘We have further to go,’ says Huw Pill after increase to 4% this month as Bank seeks to tackle rising inflation

The Bank of England will probably need to raise interest rates next month and again in early 2027 to combat rising inflation, its chief economist has said.

Signalling a sharp rise in mortgage payments for an estimated 2.3 million homeowners who will have to refinance their loans next year, Huw Pill said that while the decision to nudge interest rates from 3.75% to 4% earlier this month was a “significant step” towards getting monetary policy into a better place, “we ⁠have further to go”.

items.summary:

But at the bottom of the sign, in smaller letters, it read: “Will any state end vaccine markets?” It was accompanied by the logo for Polymarket, an online prediction market where users can log in to wager on the outcomes of nearly any event – including, now, public health.

items.title: Fight the climate crisis or go for growth? There is a way Burnham can do both | Jonathan Freedland
items.summary:
The environmental and economic dilemmas he faces are formidable but, with a bold plan, he could set an example for leaders around the world

For politicians of the centre-left especially, it’s the great dilemma of the age. How do you do what everyone can see is essential to save the planet from boiling – even as your voters demand action to get the economy growing and to make life more affordable? Plenty of activists will tell you there’s no contradiction, that tackling the climate crisis makes economic as well as ecological sense and, in the long term, you know they’re right. But you don’t live in the long term. You’re running the government right now and facing several unavoidable, binary choices.

Andy Burnham is a prime example. This week, he addressed the Cop summit in Antalya, promising “a new era of British leadership” in the struggle against global heating. It’s important to him to talk that way: his political strategy relies on shrinking the appeal of the Green party, whose electoral success earlier this year helped remove his predecessor. But talk only takes you so far. Eventually the words have to be matched by action.

Jonathan Freedland is a Guardian columnist
